newsitem.title: USA: Congress, industry eye Superfund reform.
newsitem.headline: Congress, industry eye Superfund reform.

text.p: With election politics behind it, Congress could break a logjam next year to reform the multibillion dollar federal toxic waste cleanup program, Congressional and industry officials said Friday.

Attempts to rewrite the Superfund law this year came to a standstill in a hail of blame and rhetoric, with Republicans and Democrats refusing to agree on the key issue of who should pay to clean up toxic dumps.
But industry and Congressional officials suggested the new bipartisan mood could prevail and might lead to a more moderate plan to overhaul liability and cleanup standards.

"I think the fact that the the election is behind us will take pressure off all the negotiating parties," said Jeff Merrifield, an aide to New Hampshire Republican Sen. Bob Smith, chairman of the Senate Superfund panel.

Merrifield said he expected Superfund to remain a priority for Smith in the new Congress. House Commerce Committee chairman Rep. Thomas Bliley, a Virginia Republican, similarly said Superfund would be at the top of his agenda.
"I can think of no higher goal for next year than comprehensive Superfund reform," he said, according to the written text of a speech he gave in Richmond on Friday.
Insurance industry officials, who demanded that all companies which dumped waste legally before 1981 should be let off the liability hook, acknowledged they would not get their way next year.
"Maybe we're not going to get as many as the Alliance would like to see out of the (liability) system," said Julie Rochman, spokeswoman for the Alliance of American Insurers.
"People are scaling back their expectations ... and being more realistic on what is achievable," said Owen Kean, a spokesman for the Chemical Manufacturers Association.

Industry groups and Congressional aides said the tone of Superfund talks would depend on who took the lead on the Republican side: Rep. Michael Oxley of Ohio, who led the debate this year, or Rep. Sherwood Boehlert of New York, a moderate on environmental issues.
Sen. Smith's aide dismissed environmentalists' suggestions that Smith might be cowed in Superfund negotiations, having barely survived his election.
"The environment was not a defining issue in this campaign," Merrifield said.
Smith would likely want to resume negotiations where they left off in the summer, he said.
